name: Winckley Square
text: Your train passes near Winckley Square, on the train's {side}, laid out from 1801 as an exclusive place to live for Preston's gentry. Its gardens, once private plots for each house, are now a public park with a statue of Sir Robert Peel put up in 1852.

name: West Cliff, Preston
text: Your train passes near West Cliff, on the train's {side}, a cricket ground where the first recorded match was played in 1870. Lancashire played first-class matches here in the 1930s and in 1952, and it is still the home of Preston Cricket Club.

name: Irongate
text: Your train passes near Irongate, on the train's {side}, home of Bamber Bridge Football Club. Its record crowd of 2,300 came in 1996, when the Czech Republic, training here before Euro 96, played a friendly against the club and won nine goals to one.

name: Farington Cricket Ground
text: Your train passes near Farington Cricket Ground, on the train's {side}, which opened in 2026 as a second home for Lancashire County Cricket Club. Its design was loosely based on the Hagley Oval in Christchurch, New Zealand.

name: Buckshaw Hall
text: Your train passes near Buckshaw Hall, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house built in 1654. In 1936 the estate was sold to the Ministry of Supply for the ROF Chorley munitions factory, and the hall was used as offices.

name: Preston England Temple
text: Your train passes near the Preston England Temple, on the train's {side}, which despite its name is in Chorley. It was the second temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints built in Great Britain; the church's first missionaries arrived in Preston in 1837.

name: St George's Church, Chorley
text: Your train passes near St George's Church, on the train's {side}, built between 1822 and 1825 to a design by Thomas Rickman. It was a Commissioners' church, paid for partly by a grant from the Church Building Commission.

name: Christ Church, Adlington
text: Your train passes near Christ Church, on the train's {side}, a Neo-Norman church of 1838 to 1839. It was declared redundant in 1980, and by 2013 it had become a restaurant.

name: Toughsheet Community Stadium
text: Your train passes near the Toughsheet Community Stadium, on the train's {side}, home of Bolton Wanderers. It opened in 1997 as the Reebok Stadium, replacing Burnden Park, and has a hotel built into it, with some rooms looking out over the pitch.

name: Lostock Hall Gatehouse
text: Your train passes near Lostock Hall Gatehouse, on the train's {side}, an Elizabethan gatehouse bearing the royal arms of Elizabeth I and the date 1591. The hall it once led to was pulled down in 1816 and 1824, and the gatehouse is all that remains.

name: Wingates
text: Your train passes near Wingates, on the train's {side}, a small settlement above Westhoughton whose name is thought to mean "a gate for the wind". It is the home of the Wingates Band, one of the best-known brass bands in the United Kingdom.

name: Westhoughton
text: Your train passes near Westhoughton, on the train's {side}, whose people are sometimes called "Keaw-yeds" (cow heads). The folk tale behind it tells of a farmer who found his cow with its head stuck in a gate and cut off the head rather than damage the gate.

name: Christ Church, Ince-in-Makerfield
text: Your train passes near Christ Church, on the train's {side}, built between 1861 and 1864 to a design by the Lancaster architect E. G. Paley, with a chancel ending in a many-sided apse.

name: Trencherfield Mill
text: Your train passes near Trencherfield Mill, on the train's {side}, a cotton mill of 1907 beside the Leeds and Liverpool Canal. Its 2,500 horsepower steam engine, whose two halves are called Rina and Helen, has been restored and can still be seen in steam on some days.

name: Site of Westwood Power Station
text: Your train passes near the site of Westwood Power Station, on the train's {side}, a coal-fired station built from 1948 beside the Leeds and Liverpool Canal. Its two cooling towers came down in 1989, and much of the site is now a business park.

name: Garswood
text: Your train passes near Garswood, on the train's {side}, a village whose name comes from the Old English for "fir wood". In 1588 the area's first free grammar school was founded here, and its site is now the village library.

name: Carr Mill Dam
text: Your train passes near Carr Mill Dam, on the train's {side}, at 55 acres the largest stretch of inland water in the area. Once a mill pond, it was enlarged in the 1750s to feed the Sankey Brook Navigation, and it is the home of the Lancashire Powerboat Racing Club, founded in 1923.

name: World of Glass
text: Your train passes near the World of Glass, on the train's {side}, a museum of St Helens and its glassmaking. It stands beside Pilkington's Jubilee tank house, a brick cone built in 1887 to hold the first ever continuous glassmaking furnace.

name: Our Lady Help of Christians Church, Portico
text: Your train passes near Our Lady Help of Christians Church, on the train's {side}, founded in 1790 by the Jesuits. For more than 60 years it was the only Catholic church in the area, until a second was built in the centre of Prescot in 1856.

name: Flat Iron Building, Prescot
text: Your train passes near the Flat Iron Building, on the train's {side}, built in 1890 as a workshop and warehouse for the Lancashire Watch Company. Until the late 19th century Prescot was the English centre of watchmaking.

name: Huyton & Prescot Golf Club
text: Your train passes near Huyton & Prescot Golf Club, on the train's {side}, a parkland course first laid out by James Braid. It was founded in 1905 on Hurst Park, the old estate of the Atherton family.

name: Huyton Municipal Building
text: Your train passes near Huyton Municipal Building, on the train's {side}, headquarters of Knowsley Council. It opened in 1963, and an eight-storey block in bands of brown brick and glass was added in 1973 and 1974.

name: Site of Court Hey Hall
text: Your train passes near the site of Court Hey Hall, on the train's {side}, a mansion built for Robertson Gladstone, elder brother of the Prime Minister William Gladstone. It was pulled down in 1956, and part of its grounds became Court Hey Park.

name: Tate & Lyle Sugar Silo
text: Your train passes near the Tate & Lyle Sugar Silo, on the train's {side}, a huge concrete store built from 1955 to 1957 beside Huskisson Dock. Sugar was carried up from the ships by conveyor and spread along the silo by an overhead railway; it is still in use.

name: Royal Liver Building
text: Your train passes near the Royal Liver Building, on the train's {side}, finished in 1911 at the Pier Head. A copper Liver bird stands on each of its clock towers, and its clock faces are larger than those of Big Ben.

name: Kirkdale TMD
text: Your train passes near Kirkdale depot, on the train's {side}, the largest depot on the Merseyrail network, where its trains are stabled, cleaned and maintained. It is also the United Kingdom headquarters of the train builder Stadler.

name: Statue of Edward VII, Bootle
text: Your train passes near a bronze statue of Edward VII, on the train's {side}, in King's Gardens. It marks his coronation and was unveiled by Lady Derby in 1904, on land given to the borough by Lord Derby.

name: Liverpool Metropolitan Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Liverpool Metropolitan Cathedral, on the train's {side}, built between 1962 and 1967 to Frederick Gibberd's winning design in a worldwide competition. Locals nickname it "Paddy's Wigwam" or "the Mersey Funnel".

name: Greenbank Drive Synagogue
text: Your train passes near the former Greenbank Drive Synagogue, on the train's {side}, built in the Art Deco style and opened in 1937 as Liverpool's Jewish community moved out towards Sefton Park. It closed in 2008.

name: Littlewoods Pools building
text: Your train passes near the Littlewoods Pools building, on the train's {side}, built in 1938 as the headquarters of the football pools firm. In the Second World War it housed the postal censors, and floors for Halifax bombers were made here.

name: Monk's Well
text: Your train passes near Monk's Well, on the train's {side}, a holy well inscribed with the date 1414. Its Latin inscription roughly means "He who here does nought bestow, the Devil laughs at him below", a reminder to visitors to give alms.

name: Robin Hood's Stone
text: Your train passes near Robin Hood's Stone, on the train's {side}, a Bronze Age standing stone with cup marks, moved to its street corner in 1928. Legend says medieval archers sharpened their arrows on its grooves, though there is no evidence for it.

name: 20 Forthlin Road
text: Your train passes near 20 Forthlin Road, on the train's {side}, the house where Paul McCartney lived from 1955. The Beatles wrote and rehearsed their earliest songs here, and it has belonged to the National Trust since 1995.

name: Cressington railway station
text: Cressington station, at one end of this stretch, is a listed building that opened in 1864. Its platforms are narrower than usual: lengthening them for six-car trains was hard, as the station sits in a narrow cutting between two bridges.

name: Aigburth Cricket Ground
text: Your train passes near Aigburth Cricket Ground, on the train's {side}, home of Liverpool Cricket Club since 1880. Its pavilion is the oldest still standing at a first-class cricket ground.

name: St Michael's Church, Aigburth
text: Your train passes near St Michael-in-the-Hamlet, on the train's {side}, a church of 1813 to 1815 built by the iron founder John Cragg. Historic England calls it one of the earliest and most thorough uses of industrial materials in a major building, for all the cast iron in it.

name: Toxteth Unitarian Chapel
text: Your train passes near the Ancient Chapel of Toxteth, on the train's {side}, where the young Richard Mather preached his first sermon in 1618, before emigrating to America in 1635. It is still used as a Unitarian chapel.

name: Liverpool Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Liverpool Cathedral, on the train's {side}, Britain's largest cathedral and the longest in the world. Built to a design by Giles Gilbert Scott, it took from 1904 to 1978 to finish.
